question: Which projection sends x-rays from posterior to anterior through the patient?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss differences in chest x-ray (CXR) quality between PA (PosteroAnterior) erect and AP (AnteroPosterior) supine CXR's

options.rationale: A PA projection directs x-rays from posterior to anterior and provides a higher-quality examination when the patient can stand.
An AP projection directs x-rays from anterior to posterior. It would be correct if the beam entered the anterior chest first.
An AP semi-erect image still uses an anterior-to-posterior beam. It would be correct if anterior beam entry were described.
A decubitus examination describes side-lying positioning rather than posterior-to-anterior beam travel. It would be correct if dependent pleural fluid were being evaluated.
A left decubitus examination describes positioning rather than a posterior-to-anterior projection. It would be correct if nondependent right pleural air were being demonstrated.

question: Which structure forms the anterior cardiac border on a lateral chest radiograph?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and discuss normal and abnormal cardiomediastinal contours on PA and lateral CXR

options.rationale: The left atrium forms much of the posterior heart border. It would be correct if the posterior cardiac contour were identified.
The left ventricle is visible as part of the heart but does not form the stated anterior border. It would be correct for the corresponding left-sided contour on a PA image.
The heart is primarily anterior in the thorax, and the right ventricle forms its anterior border on the lateral projection.
The right atrium contributes to the right cardiomediastinal contour on a PA image. It would be correct if that frontal contour were tested.
The superior vena cava contributes to the upper right mediastinal contour rather than the anterior cardiac border. It would be correct for that PA contour.

question: Which finding defines cardiomegaly on an adequately obtained adult PA chest radiograph?
cited_learning_objective: Determine cardiomegaly on a CXR

options.rationale: A ratio below 40% does not meet the enlargement threshold. It would represent a cardiac shadow well below the stated cutoff.
A ratio of 40% remains below the threshold for cardiomegaly. It would be compatible with a nonenlarged cardiac shadow.
A ratio below 50% is normal for adults and older children on PA imaging. It would be correct if normal heart size were requested.
The stated abnormal criterion is greater than 50%, not equal to 50%. A value above this boundary would make cardiomegaly the correct interpretation.
On an adult PA radiograph, a cardiothoracic ratio greater than 50% indicates an enlarged cardiac shadow consistent with cardiomegaly.

question: Which modality is the most commonly used cross-sectional imaging study of the heart?
cited_learning_objective: Identify the most commonly utilized cross-sectional imaging modality to evaluate the heart

options.rationale: Coronary CTA is a noninvasive method for imaging coronary arteries. It would be correct if a coronary artery technique were requested.
Echocardiography is the most commonly used cross-sectional imaging study of the heart.
Catheterization is the definitive coronary artery imaging study rather than the most common cross-sectional cardiac study. It would be correct if definitive coronary imaging were requested.
Chest radiography produces a projection image rather than a cross-sectional cardiac study. It would be correct for initial thoracic projection imaging.
Supine radiography is a lower-quality projection technique used when a patient cannot stand. It is not cross-sectional imaging.

question: A frontal chest image shows the spinous processes equidistant from the medial clavicular ends and displays 10 posterior ribs. Which interpretation of image quality is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss factors affecting the CXR appearance of the cardiomediastinal shadow

options.rationale: This interpretation combines both stated quality criteria, but it is not the keyed option because the option set requires the single best description of the two findings together. This option creates a second key and therefore cannot be retained.
Equidistance of the spinous process from the medial clavicles indicates absence of substantial rotation. This would be correct if those distances were unequal.
Ten visible posterior ribs indicate good inspiration rather than shallow inspiration. This would be correct if fewer posterior ribs were visible.
Clavicular symmetry indicates adequate alignment, while visualization of 10 posterior ribs indicates good inspiration.
Neither component matches the findings. Unequal clavicular distances and reduced rib visualization would support this interpretation.

question: A cardiac shadow measures 15 cm, and the inferior inner thoracic width measures 28 cm on a PA image. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: Determine cardiomegaly on a CXR

options.rationale: The cardiothoracic ratio is approximately 54%, which exceeds the 50% threshold for cardiomegaly on a PA image.
Cardiac width must be compared with thoracic width rather than interpreted alone. This would be correct if the calculated ratio were below 50%.
Thoracic width alone does not establish heart size. This would support normal size only if the cardiac-to-thoracic proportion were below 50%.
The cardiothoracic ratio assesses cardiac shadow size, not rotation. Unequal distances between the spinous process and medial clavicles would indicate rotation.
Cardiac width alone cannot diagnose shallow inspiration. Reduced visualization below 10 posterior or 6-7 anterior ribs would support that quality defect.

question: A chest radiograph shows a smooth contour at the distal aortic arch followed inferiorly by the pulmonary trunk contour. Which additional structure normally continues the left cardiomediastinal border?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and discuss normal and abnormal cardiomediastinal contours on PA and lateral CXR

options.rationale: The right atrium contributes to the right border rather than the left border. It would be correct if the inferior right contour were requested.
The superior vena cava contributes to the upper right mediastinal border. It would be correct for the superior right contour.
The left-sided sequence includes the aortic knob, main pulmonary artery, and left ventricle.
The right ventricle forms the anterior cardiac border on the lateral view rather than the left PA contour. It would be correct for that lateral relationship.
The left atrium forms much of the posterior heart border on the lateral view. It would be correct if that posterior relationship were tested.

question: Two frontal images of the same patient are obtained one day apart. The portable supine image shows a wider central shadow than the standing image. Which factor best explains the difference?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss factors affecting the CXR appearance of the cardiomediastinal shadow

options.rationale: Posterior rib visibility assesses inspiration and does not specifically explain projection-related enlargement. Reduced rib visibility would instead suggest shallow inspiration.
Anterior rib count also evaluates inspiration rather than the stated projection difference. Six to seven visible anterior ribs would indicate good inspiration.
Reduced rotation would lessen distortion rather than systematically enlarge the central shadow. Unequal clavicular distances would make rotation relevant.
Pleural fluid distribution changes with position but does not explain generalized accentuation of the cardiomediastinal shadow. It would be relevant to effusion appearance.
An AP supine technique accentuates the cardiomediastinal shadow compared with a PA erect technique.

question: A fluid collection moves to the dependent lateral pleural space when a patient lies on one side. Which imaging approach uses this behavior to improve detection and quantification?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the effect of patient positioning (erect vs. supine vs. decubitus) on CXR detection and appearance of pleural effusion and pneumothorax

options.rationale: On a supine image, fluid layers posteriorly and may create a veiling opacity. This would be correct if posterior layering were the desired appearance.
A side-down decubitus image places pleural fluid laterally in the dependent space, improving detection and estimation.
Erect imaging makes fluid collect inferiorly with a meniscus. It would be correct if inferior costophrenic blunting were being sought.
An erect lateral image can show posterior costophrenic blunting but does not use lateral dependent layering. It would be correct for evaluating posterior recess fluid.
This is not the described problem-solving technique for lateral fluid layering. A side-down decubitus position is required for that distribution.

question: Which paired distribution correctly describes pleural contents in an upright patient?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the effect of patient positioning (erect vs. supine vs. decubitus) on CXR detection and appearance of pleural effusion and pneumothorax

options.rationale: This reverses the effects of gravity. It would be correct only if air behaved dependently and fluid nondependently.
This does not describe the principal upright distribution. Posterior fluid layering is expected in a supine patient.
Lateral air collection is associated with an appropriate decubitus position, not the standard upright distribution. Medial fluid is not the stated dependent pattern.
Pleural air rises to a nondependent location, whereas pleural fluid descends to the dependent inferior pleural space.
This directly reverses the governing relationship. It would become correct only if the labels for air and fluid were exchanged.

question: A peripheral thoracic lucency lies beyond a thin line marking the edge of a partially collapsed lung. Which additional finding should occur in that peripheral region?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss and recognize pleural effusion, pneumothorax, and tension pneumothorax on CXR

options.rationale: Pleural air lies peripheral to the visceral pleural line, so lung markings are absent in that lucent region.
Visible markings identify aerated lung on the hilar side of the pleural line. They would be expected within the partially collapsed lung.
A meniscus reflects dependent pleural fluid rather than pleural air. It would be correct for an erect pleural effusion.
A veiling opacity reflects posteriorly layered fluid on a supine image. It would be correct for a supine pleural effusion.
Costophrenic blunting is an early sign of dependent pleural fluid. It would be correct if an effusion occupied the costodiaphragmatic recess.

question: A normal frontal image shows a slightly higher left hilum than right. Most of the density producing these contours comes from which structures?
cited_learning_objective: Correlate thoracic anatomy with medical imaging

options.rationale: The bronchi are related to the hila but do not create most of the normal hilar density. This would be relevant if airway anatomy were being localized.
Normal lymph nodes do not account for most hilar density. Enlarged bilateral hilar nodes would instead create abnormal hilar enlargement.
Most normal hilar density on a PA chest image is produced by the pulmonary arteries.
The provided normal hilar emphasis is on pulmonary arteries rather than veins. This option would require a source description assigning most hilar density to veins.
Hilar fat is not identified as the major source of normal hilar density. This would require a fat-dominant contour rather than the normal vascular contour.

question: A method rapidly injects contrast through a vein and then performs rapid computed scanning to display coronary vessels. Which technique is described?
cited_learning_objective: Identify 2 techniques that image the coronary arteries

options.rationale: Catheter angiography advances a catheter through the arterial system and injects contrast into coronary arteries. It would be correct if arterial catheter advancement were described.
PA radiography does not use rapid intravenous contrast followed by CT scanning. It would be correct for a routine high-quality frontal chest image.
AP radiography is a projection technique often used portably and does not directly display coronary arteries. It would be correct for a patient unable to stand.
Echocardiography is the common cross-sectional heart study but is not the described contrast-enhanced CT coronary technique.
Coronary artery CTA is a noninvasive technique using rapid intravenous contrast injection followed by rapid CT scanning.

question: An investigator compares thoracic images obtained at full inspiration and shallow inspiration in the same subject. Which paired change is expected with shallow inspiration?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss factors affecting the CXR appearance of the cardiomediastinal shadow

options.rationale: This pairing is correct because shallow inspiration reduces visible rib count and accentuates the cardiac shadow. Retaining it as incorrect would create a second key.
The rib change is appropriate, but shallow inspiration makes the heart appear larger rather than smaller. A smaller appearance would not match the stated effect.
More visible ribs indicate better inspiration. This would require good inspiration rather than shallow inspiration.
Shallow inspiration reduces the number of visible ribs and accentuates the cardiomediastinal shadow.
More ribs are associated with good inspiration, while the described shallow study has reduced expansion. This would require a well-inspired image.

question: A patient has enlargement of the cardiac silhouette on a technically adequate PA image. Which process can mimic true cardiac enlargement without requiring enlargement of the heart itself?
cited_learning_objective: Determine cardiomegaly on a CXR

options.rationale: Hilar lymphadenopathy enlarges the hila rather than the cardiac silhouette. It would be correct if bilateral hilar enlargement were present.
An aortic aneurysm can produce a prominent aortic knob rather than generalized cardiac-shadow enlargement. It would be correct for that focal contour abnormality.
Shallow inspiration can accentuate the shadow, but the stem specifies a technically adequate PA image. It would be correct if reduced rib visualization showed poor inspiration.
Rotation distorts cardiomediastinal contours, but adequate technique excludes this explanation. It would be correct with unequal clavicular distances.
Pericardial effusion can enlarge the cardiac shadow and thereby mimic cardiomegaly on chest radiography.

question: A 72-year-old patient cannot stand after an injury. A portable frontal image shows an enlarged central shadow, but the medial clavicular ends are symmetric and only 5 anterior ribs are visible. Which action best prevents overcalling cardiac enlargement?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss factors affecting the CXR appearance of the cardiomediastinal shadow

options.rationale: An AP supine technique and shallow inspiration both accentuate the cardiomediastinal shadow, so these factors must be considered before diagnosing cardiomegaly.
Symmetric medial clavicular distances argue against substantial rotation. This would be correct if the spinous process were unequally positioned between the clavicles.
The shadow is affected by two technical magnifiers, so immediate diagnosis risks a false-positive interpretation. This would be appropriate only after excluding projection and inspiratory effects.
Hilar disease alters hilar density or symmetry rather than uniformly explaining this technically accentuated central shadow. Abnormal hilar masses would support this choice.
Pericardial fluid can mimic cardiomegaly, but the stem supplies technical explanations that must be addressed first. This would require persistent enlargement on an adequate PA study.

question: A 64-year-old patient with pneumonia develops a left inferior hemithorax opacity. An erect image shows an upward-curving upper margin and loss of the normally acute lateral recess. Which diagnosis best explains these findings?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss and recognize pleural effusion, pneumothorax, and tension pneumothorax on CXR

options.rationale: A pneumothorax produces peripheral lucency without lung markings rather than dependent opacity with a meniscus. It would be correct if pleural air and a visceral pleural line were present.
Dependent pleural fluid on an erect image produces costophrenic angle blunting and a meniscus.
Tension pneumothorax produces pleural lucency plus mass effect rather than an inferior meniscus. It would be correct with contralateral mediastinal shift and a depressed ipsilateral hemidiaphragm.
Hilar lymphadenopathy enlarges the hilar contour rather than filling the inferior pleural recess. It would be correct if central hilar enlargement were shown.
An aortic aneurysm produces prominence of the aortic knob rather than an inferior pleural meniscus. It would be correct for focal upper left mediastinal contour enlargement.

question: A 58-year-old supine patient has shortness of breath. A portable image shows a diffuse right-sided veiling opacity with pulmonary vessels still visible and no meniscus. Which explanation is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the effect of patient positioning (erect vs. supine vs. decubitus) on CXR detection and appearance of pleural effusion and pneumothorax

options.rationale: Pleural air causes increased lucency rather than a veiling opacity. It would be correct if a subtle supine pneumothorax were being considered.
Inferior pooling with a meniscus occurs in an erect patient. It would be correct if the patient were upright and the costophrenic angle were blunted.
In a supine patient, pleural fluid layers posteriorly and may create a veiling opacity through which lung markings remain visible.
Lateral pleural air is expected when the affected side is nondependent during decubitus imaging. It would produce lucency without peripheral lung markings.
Enlarged hilar structures create central contour abnormalities rather than a unilateral veiling opacity. Central bilateral enlargement would make this choice appropriate.

question: A 45-year-old supine patient has suspected pleural fluid, but portable radiography is indeterminate. The patient cannot stand. Which next study best uses positional redistribution to detect and estimate the collection?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the effect of patient positioning (erect vs. supine vs. decubitus) on CXR detection and appearance of pleural effusion and pneumothorax

options.rationale: Repeating the same insensitive position would again allow posterior layering. It would be appropriate for comparison, but not for exploiting redistribution.
Erect PA imaging would show inferior fluid well, but the patient cannot stand. It would be correct if erect positioning were tolerated.
An erect lateral view can demonstrate posterior recess fluid, but it also requires erect positioning. It would be correct if the patient could tolerate standing.
A side-down decubitus image causes mobile fluid to layer laterally, making it useful for detecting and quantifying an effusion.
This does not provide the established lateral dependent layering used for problem solving. A side-down decubitus position is required.

question: A 20-year-old woman develops abrupt pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea. An erect image shows a thin peripheral line with lucency beyond it and no vascular markings. Which process produced the imaging abnormality?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss and recognize pleural effusion, pneumothorax, and tension pneumothorax on CXR

options.rationale: Pleural fluid produces dependent opacity, costophrenic blunting, or a meniscus rather than peripheral lucency. Those findings would make this correct.
Mediastinal fat can mimic cardiac enlargement but does not create a visceral pleural line. A broad enlarged central shadow would support this choice.
Hilar lymphadenopathy creates central hilar enlargement rather than peripheral avascular lucency. Bilateral hilar masses would make this correct.
Pericardial fluid may enlarge the cardiac silhouette but does not separate the lung from the chest wall. An enlarged cardiac shadow would support this option.
A pleural breach permits air to enter, alters negative intrapleural pressure, and allows elastic recoil to collapse the lung toward the hilum.

question: A 35-year-old woman undergoes supine imaging after a bicycle fall. The image is equivocal for a small pleural air collection, and she cannot tolerate standing. Which study is a more sensitive alternative that does not require transport to radiology?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the effect of patient positioning (erect vs. supine vs. decubitus) on CXR detection and appearance of pleural effusion and pneumothorax

options.rationale: Bedside ultrasound is more sensitive than supine chest radiography for pneumothorax when performed by an experienced physician and avoids transport.
Supine radiography remains relatively insensitive for pneumothorax. It would be appropriate only if no more sensitive bedside study were available.
An erect PA image is more revealing, but the patient cannot tolerate standing. It would be correct if erect positioning were possible.
Coronary CTA evaluates coronary arteries rather than pleural air. It would be correct for noninvasive coronary vessel imaging.
Catheter angiography is definitive for coronary arteries, not pneumothorax. It would be correct if invasive coronary assessment were required.

question: A 40-year-old patient with pleuritic pain has normal shimmering movement of the pleural interface beneath the probe at the symptomatic site. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss and recognize pleural effusion, pneumothorax, and tension pneumothorax on CXR

options.rationale: Visible lung sliding argues strongly against pneumothorax at that location. Absence of sliding with supportive findings would raise concern.

options.text: Pleural effusion confirmed at probe site
options.rationale: Lung sliding represents visceral and parietal pleural apposition rather than an anechoic fluid collection. Fluid above the diaphragm would support effusion.
Lung sliding represents visceral pleura moving along parietal pleura and effectively rules out pneumothorax at the probe location.

options.text: Tension physiology confirmed at probe site
options.rationale: Lung sliding does not demonstrate positive intrapleural pressure or mass effect. Contralateral mediastinal shift and diaphragmatic depression would support tension physiology.
A local ultrasound finding applies only at the site examined. Pleural air elsewhere would require scanning appropriate additional locations.

question: A 29-year-old patient has absent pleural-interface movement during bedside ultrasonography after chest trauma. Which conclusion is justified by this finding alone?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss and recognize pleural effusion, pneumothorax, and tension pneumothorax on CXR

options.rationale: Absence of lung sliding is nonspecific because other conditions can also produce it. Additional supportive findings would be required.
Absent sliding does not establish pleural fluid. Anechoic fluid located above the diaphragm would support an effusion.
Normal apposition is supported by visible sliding rather than its absence. Shimmering movement with respiration would make this correct.
Absent lung sliding raises the possibility of pneumothorax but is nonspecific and cannot independently confirm the diagnosis.
Visible lung sliding, not absent sliding, effectively excludes pneumothorax at the probe site. Demonstrated sliding would make this correct.

question: A 33-year-old patient becomes acutely dyspneic after chest trauma. Imaging shows left pleural lucency without vascular markings, collapse of the left lung, rightward displacement of central structures, and a lowered left diaphragm. Which diagnosis is most likely?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss and recognize pleural effusion, pneumothorax, and tension pneumothorax on CXR

options.rationale: An effusion produces opacity rather than avascular lucency. A meniscus or dependent fluid opacity would make this correct.
The abnormality is lucent and left-sided rather than an opaque right-sided fluid collection. Right dependent opacity would support this diagnosis.
A right tension pneumothorax would produce right pleural air and leftward mediastinal displacement. The findings show the opposite laterality.
A simple pneumothorax can collapse the lung but lacks the described mass effect. Absence of mediastinal shift and diaphragmatic depression would support this choice.
Pleural air with ipsilateral lung collapse, contralateral mediastinal shift, and depression of the ipsilateral hemidiaphragm identifies tension pneumothorax.

question: A 33-year-old patient has severe respiratory distress after trauma. Imaging demonstrates pleural air with contralateral mediastinal displacement and depression of the ipsilateral diaphragm. Which next step is required?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss and recognize pleural effusion, pneumothorax, and tension pneumothorax on CXR

options.rationale: Tension pneumothorax is a life-threatening emergency caused by positive pleural pressure and mass effect, requiring immediate evacuation of pleural air.
Additional routine imaging delays treatment after tension findings are established. It would be appropriate for evaluating a stable suspected pneumothorax.
Coronary CTA evaluates coronary arteries and does not relieve positive pleural pressure. It would be correct for noninvasive coronary imaging.
Thoracentesis is described for drainage of pleural fluid, not emergent evacuation of tension pleural air. A sizable effusion would make this appropriate.
Coronary angiography evaluates coronary stenosis and does not treat pleural mass effect. Suspected critical coronary disease would make it relevant.

question: A 61-year-old supine patient has an indeterminate right-sided opacity. Bedside imaging identifies an anechoic collection above the diaphragm. Which next step can the same modality directly facilitate?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss and recognize pleural effusion, pneumothorax, and tension pneumothorax on CXR

options.rationale: Pleural ultrasound does not guide coronary catheterization. Arterial catheter advancement to the coronary origins would be required for that procedure.
Ultrasound can localize pleural fluid, mark a drainage site, and guide thoracentesis.
The identified abnormality is anechoic fluid rather than pleural air under positive pressure. Tension findings would require immediate decompression.
The collection is pleural and above the diaphragm, not an aortic contour abnormality. A prominent aortic knob with CT confirmation would support an aneurysm.
The modality is being used to guide pleural drainage, not intervention on hilar nodes. Bilateral hilar enlargement would indicate nodal pathology.

question: A 69-year-old patient has complete right hemithorax opacification. The mediastinum is displaced toward the left. Which process best accounts for both findings?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss and recognize pleural effusion, pneumothorax, and tension pneumothorax on CXR

options.rationale: A massive right pleural effusion can opacify the entire right hemithorax and exert mass effect that displaces the mediastinum leftward.
A small effusion causes costophrenic blunting rather than complete white-out and major displacement. Limited inferior fluid would make this correct.
A pneumothorax creates pleural lucency rather than complete opacification. A visceral pleural line with absent peripheral markings would support it.
Although tension can shift the mediastinum leftward, it produces a lucent right pleural space rather than white-out. Avascular lucency would make this correct.
Hilar lymphadenopathy enlarges central hilar contours and does not opacify an entire hemithorax. Bilateral central masses would support this diagnosis.

question: A 70-year-old patient has an unusually prominent upper left mediastinal contour. Subsequent cross-sectional imaging shows pathologic dilation of the corresponding vessel. Which abnormality was present?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and discuss normal and abnormal cardiomediastinal contours on PA and lateral CXR

options.rationale: The main pulmonary artery contour lies below the distal aortic arch contour. Enlargement at that lower contour would support this choice.
The superior vena cava contributes to the right upper mediastinal contour rather than the upper left contour. Right-sided prominence would be required.
The descending thoracic aorta is seen along a different contour than the upper left aortic knob. Dilation localized to the descending segment would support this choice.
A prominent aortic knob can reflect an aneurysm involving the distal aspect of the aortic arch.
The right atrium forms an inferior right cardiac contour rather than an upper left mediastinal contour. Right lower border enlargement would support this option.

question: A 52-year-old patient has symmetric enlargement of both hilar contours on frontal and lateral images. The normal vascular relationships are obscured by enlarged nodal tissue. Which diagnosis best matches this pattern?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and discuss normal and abnormal cardiomediastinal contours on PA and lateral CXR

options.rationale: Pathologically enlarged lymph nodes produce bilateral hilar enlargement beyond the normal pulmonary arterial contours.
The abnormality is symmetric and bilateral rather than confined to one hilum. One-sided nodal enlargement would make this correct.
Normal hila are primarily vascular, with the left often slightly higher, but they should not contain enlarged nodal tissue. Absence of a mass would support normality.
Aortic knob prominence affects the upper left mediastinal contour, not both hila. Focal upper left contour enlargement would make this correct.
Cardiac enlargement increases the cardiac shadow rather than producing discrete bilateral hilar masses. A cardiothoracic ratio above 50% on PA imaging would support it.

question: A 76-year-old patient has an elevated right hemidiaphragm and a right apical pulmonary mass. Which anatomic relationship best links these findings?
cited_learning_objective: Correlate thoracic anatomy with medical imaging

options.rationale: The provided imaging relationship attributes diaphragmatic elevation to phrenic nerve involvement, not vagal involvement. A different functional consequence would be needed for this option.
The mass and elevated diaphragm are right-sided, and the implicated nerve is not the vagus. A left-sided non-diaphragmatic finding would be required.
A right apical mass can impinge on the right phrenic nerve and produce abnormal elevation of the right hemidiaphragm.
Left phrenic involvement would be expected to affect the left hemidiaphragm, not the right. A left-sided diaphragmatic elevation would make this correct.
Pulmonary arterial impingement does not explain the stated nerve-related diaphragmatic elevation. A hilar vascular contour abnormality would make it relevant.

question: A 59-year-old patient requires definitive imaging of suspected severe coronary narrowing because the result will directly influence treatment. Which procedure is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: Identify 2 techniques that image the coronary arteries

options.rationale: PA radiography evaluates thoracic projection anatomy but does not definitively display coronary artery lumens. It would be appropriate for general chest assessment.
AP radiography is a lower-quality portable chest technique and does not define coronary stenosis. It would be appropriate when the patient cannot stand.
Echocardiography is the most common cross-sectional heart study, but it is not identified as the definitive coronary artery examination.
Coronary CTA images coronary arteries noninvasively, but the definitive study specified for treatment-guiding coronary assessment is catheterization.
Coronary catheterization is the definitive coronary artery imaging study, and its findings strongly influence treatment decisions.

question: A 63-year-old patient undergoes a noninvasive coronary study. Contrast is rapidly injected into a peripheral vein before rapid scanning. Which mechanism produces the vascular images?
cited_learning_objective: Identify 2 techniques that image the coronary arteries

options.rationale: Coronary CTA combines rapid intravenous contrast administration with rapid computed tomographic scanning to form coronary images.
Coronary CTA does not require an arterial catheter. Arterial catheter advancement would instead describe invasive coronary angiography.
Routine chest radiography does not provide the described cross-sectional coronary images. Rapid CT scanning after injection is required.
This does not match either coronary technique described. Catheter angiography uses arterial access and direct coronary contrast imaging.
The described noninvasive coronary technique uses CT rather than ultrasound after intravenous contrast. Echocardiography is a different cardiac modality.
